The (one-dimensional) '''Holtsmark distribution''' is a [[continuous probability distribution]]. The Holtsmark distribution is a special case of a [[stable distribution]] with the index of stability or shape parameter <math>\alpha</math> equal to 3/2 and the [[skewness]] parameter <math>\beta</math> of zero. Since <math>\beta</math> equals zero, the distribution is symmetric, and thus an example of a symmetric alpha-stable distribution. The Holtsmark distribution is one of the few examples of a stable distribution for which a closed form expression of the [[probability density function]] is known. However, its probability density function is not expressible in terms of [[elementary functions]]; rather, the probability density function is expressed in terms of [[Generalized hypergeometric function|hypergeometric functions]].

The Holtsmark distribution has applications in plasma physics and astrophysics.<ref name=lee/> In 1919, Norwegian physicist [[Johan Peter Holtsmark]] proposed the distribution as a model for the fluctuating fields in plasma due to the motion of charged particles.<ref>{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1002/andp.19193630702
| volume = 363
| issue = 7
| pages = 577–630
| last = Holtsmark
| first = J.
| title = Uber die Verbreiterung von Spektrallinien
| journal = Annalen der Physik
| year = 1919
| bibcode = 1919AnP...363..577H | url = https://zenodo.org/record/1424343
}}</ref> It is also applicable to other types of Coulomb forces, in particular to modeling of gravitating bodies, and thus is important in astrophysics.<ref>{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1086/144420
| issn = 0004-637X
| volume = 95
| pages = 489
| last = Chandrasekhar
| first = S.
|author2=J. von Neumann
| title = The Statistics of the Gravitational Field Arising from a Random Distribution of Stars. I. The Speed of Fluctuations
| journal = The Astrophysical Journal
| year = 1942
| bibcode=1942ApJ....95..489C
}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1103/RevModPhys.15.1
| volume = 15
| issue = 1

| last = Chandrasekhar

==Characteristic function==

The [[characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]] of a symmetric stable distribution is:

<math display="block">
\varphi(t;\mu,c) = 
\exp\left[~it\mu \! - \! \left|c t\right|^\alpha\right],
</math>

where <math>\alpha</math> is the shape parameter, or index of stability, <math>\mu</math> is the [[location parameter]], and ''c'' is the [[scale parameter]].

Since the Holtsmark distribution has <math>\alpha=3/2,</math> its characteristic function is:<ref name=zolotarev>{{cite book|title=One-Dimensional Stable Distributions|last=Zolotarev | first= V. M.|pages=[https://archive.org/details/onedimensionalst00zolo_0/page/1 1], 41 | year = 1986 | location=Providence, RI|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|isbn=978-0-8218-4519-6|url=https://archive.org/details/onedimensionalst00zolo_0|url-access=registration|quote=holtsmark.}}</ref>

<math display="block">
\varphi(t;\mu,c) = 
\exp\left[~it\mu \! - \! \left|c t\right|^{3/2}\right] .
</math>

Since the Holtsmark distribution is a stable distribution with {{math|''α'' > 1}}, <math>\mu</math> represents the [[mean]] of the distribution.<ref name=nolan>{{cite book|chapter=Basic Properties of Univariate Stable Distributions|title=Stable Distributions: Models for Heavy Tailed Data|author=Nolan, J. P.|pages=3, 15–16|chapter-url=http://lpmt-theory.wdfiles.com/local--files/michael-blog/stablePDF.pdf|year=2008|access-date=2011-02-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Handbook of Heavy Tailed Distributions in Finance|url=https://archive.org/details/handbookheavytai00rach_874|url-access=limited|editor=Rachev, S. T.|chapter=Modeling Financial Data|pages=[https://archive.org/details/handbookheavytai00rach_874/page/n112 111]–112|author=Nolan, J. P.|year=2003|location=Amsterdam|publisher=[[Elsevier]]|isbn=978-0-444-50896-6}}</ref> Since {{math|1=''β'' = 0}}, <math>\mu</math> also represents the [[median]] and [[Mode (statistics)|mode]] of the distribution. And since {{math|''α'' < 2}}, the [[variance]] of the Holtsmark distribution is infinite.<ref name=nolan/> All higher [[Moment (mathematics)|moments]] of the distribution are also infinite.<ref name=nolan/> Like other stable distributions (other than the normal distribution), since the variance is infinite the dispersion in the distribution is reflected by the [[scale parameter]], c. An alternate approach to describing the dispersion of the distribution is through fractional moments.<ref name=nolan/>

==Probability density function==

In general, the [[probability density function]], {{math|''f''(''x'')}}, of a continuous [[probability distribution]] can be derived from its characteristic function by:

<math display="block">
f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty \varphi(t)e^{-ixt}\,dt .
</math>

Most stable distributions do not have a known closed form expression for their probability density functions. Only the [[normal distribution|normal]], [[Cauchy distribution|Cauchy]] and [[Lévy distribution]]s have known closed form expressions in terms of [[elementary functions]].<ref name=lee/> The Holtsmark distribution is one of two symmetric stable distributions to have a known closed form expression in terms of [[generalized hypergeometric function|hypergeometric functions]].<ref name=lee/> When <math>\mu</math> is equal to 0 and the scale parameter is equal to 1, the Holtsmark distribution has the probability density function:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
f(x; 0, 1)
&= \frac{1}{\pi}\, \Gamma{\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)} \; {_2F_3}\!\left(\frac{5}{12}, \frac{11}{12}; \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{5}{6}; - \frac{4x^6}{729}\right) \\
& {} \quad{} - \frac{x^2}{3\pi} \; {_3F_4}\!\left(\frac{3}{4}, {1}, \frac{5}{4}; \frac{2}{3}, \frac{5}{6}, \frac{7}{6}, \frac{4}{3}; - \frac{4x^6}{729}\right) \\
& {} \quad{} + \frac{7x^4}{81\pi}\, \Gamma{\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)} \; {_2F_3}\!\left(\frac{13}{12}, \frac{19}{12}; \frac{7}{6}, \frac{3}{2}, \frac{5}{3}; - \frac{4x^6}{729}\right),
\end{align}</math>

where <math>{\Gamma(x)}</math> is the [[gamma function]] and <math> _mF_n(\cdot)</math> is a [[generalized hypergeometric function|hypergeometric function]].<ref name=lee>{{cite book|title=Continuous and Discrete Properties of Stochastic Processes|author=Lee, W. H.|pages=37–39|type=PhD thesis|year=2010|location=[[University of Nottingham]]|url=http://etheses.nottingham.ac.uk/11194/1/Thesis_Wai_Ha_Lee.pdf}}{{Dead link|date=August 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> One has also<ref name=pain>{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1140/epjp/s13360-020-00248-4
| volume = 135
| pages = 236
| last = Pain
| first = Jean-Christophe
| title = Expression of the Holtsmark function in terms of hypergeometric <math> _2F_2 </math> and Airy <math> \mathrm{Bi}</math> functions
| journal = Eur. Phys. J. Plus 
| year = 2020
| s2cid = 211030564
| arxiv = 2001.11893
}}</ref>

<math display="block"> \begin{align}
f(x; 0, 1) &= - \frac{x^2}{6\pi}\left[~_2F_2{\left(1, \frac{3}{2}; \frac{4}{3}, \frac{5}{3}; -\frac{4ix^3}{27}\right)} + ~{_2F_2}{\left(1, \frac{3}{2}; \frac{4}{3}, \frac{5}{3}; \frac{4ix^3}{27}\right)}\right]\\[2pt]
&\quad + \frac{4}{3^{5/3}} \left[\operatorname{Bi}'\left(-\frac{x^2}{3^{4/3}}\right) \cos\left(\frac{2x^3}{27}\right)+\frac{x}{3^{2/3}} ~ \operatorname{Bi}\left(-\frac{x^2}{3^{4/3}}\right)\sin\left(\frac{2x^3}{27}\right)\right],
\end{align}</math>

where <math> \mathrm{Bi} </math> is the Airy function of the second kind and <math> \mathrm{Bi}' </math> its derivative. The arguments of the <math> _2F_2 </math> functions are pure imaginary complex numbers, but the sum of the two functions is real. For <math> x </math> positive, the function <math> \mathrm{Bi}(-x) </math> is related to the Bessel functions of fractional order <math> J_{-1/3} </math> and <math> J_{1/3} </math> and its derivative to the Bessel functions of fractional order <math> J_{-2/3} </math> and <math> J_{2/3} </math>. Therefore, one can write<ref name=pain/>

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
f(x; 0, 1)
&= \frac{4x^2}{3^{7/2}} \cos\left(\frac{2x^3}{27}\right)\left[J_{-2/3}{\left(\frac{2x^3}{27}\right)} + J_{2/3}{\left(\frac{2x^3}{27}\right)}\right] \\[1ex]
&+ \frac{4x^2}{3^{7/2}} \sin\left(\frac{2x^3}{27}\right)\left[J_{-1/3}{\left(\frac{2x^3}{27}\right)} - J_{1/3}{\left(\frac{2x^3}{27}\right)}\right] \\[1ex]
&-\frac{x^2}{6\pi}\left[~_2F_2{\left(1, \frac{3}{2}; \frac{4}{3}, \frac{5}{3}; -\frac{4ix^3}{27}\right)} + ~_2F_2{\left(1, \frac{3}{2}; \frac{4}{3}, \frac{5}{3}; \frac{4ix^3}{27}\right)}\right].
\end{align}
</math>
